cues.text: A Fourth-Century Bishop of Lycia
As the Catholic Encyclopedia states with unusual candor, 'there is scarcely anything historically certain' about Nicholas .
Beyond that, he served as bishop of Myra , a coastal city in the Roman province of Lycia (modern southern Turkey), sometime in the fourth century.
Tradition holds he was born in the nearby city of Patara, made an early pilgrimage to Egypt and the Holy Land, and became bishop of Myra shortly after returning home.
Persecution and Council

According to the legendary accounts, Nicholas was imprisoned during the persecution of Diocletian in the early fourth century and released only after Constantine's accession brought toleration to the Church.
Some ancient lists place him among the bishops present at the Council of Nicaea in 325.
However, the Catholic Encyclopedia notes his name appears in none of the council's contemporary attendance records, leaving the tradition open to doubt.
This includes the popular later legend, unmentioned in any early source, that he struck the heretic Arius during the proceedings.
A Reputation for Secret Generosity
The stories that made Nicholas beloved across the Christian world center overwhelmingly on quiet, anonymous acts of charity.
Most famously, tradition holds, he secretly provided dowries for three poor sisters who otherwise faced destitution or worse.
He tossed gold through their window (or down the chimney, in later versions) under cover of darkness so his generosity would remain unknown to them.
A Devotion of Extraordinary Reach
Nicholas's veneration spread with remarkable speed and breadth for a bishop about whom so little could be verified.
Emperor Justinian I built a church in his honor at Constantinople as early as the sixth century.
His name entered the liturgy attributed to St. John Chrysostom, and devotion to him flourished with particular intensity in Russia and throughout the Greek East.
Translation of Relics to Bari
In 1087, Italian merchants removed Nicholas's relics from Myra, then under threat from Muslim advances into Asia Minor.
They carried them to Bari , Italy, where a basilica was built to house them.
Devotion to him in the West grew substantially, giving him the alternate title 'Nicholas of Bari.'
His feast day, December 6, has been kept ever since.
It remains one of the most widely celebrated saints' days in both the Eastern and Western Church calendars.
Legacy: From Bishop to Santa Claus
Nicholas's association with secret gift-giving to children took root especially in the Netherlands, Germany, and Switzerland.
There, the custom of leaving gifts on his feast eve carried, through Dutch settlers in New Amsterdam, into the American tradition of Santa Claus.
The fourth-century bishop of Myra thus became, by a long and winding cultural path, one of the most commercially recognizable saints in the world.
